## Definition

The **mean** (arithmetic average) is calculated by summing all values and dividing by the number of observations. It represents the "balance point" of a distribution.

## Formula

$$\bar{X} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i}{n}$$

Where:

- $\bar{X}$ = sample mean
- $X_i$ = each individual value
- $n$ = number of observations

## Properties

| Property | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| Uses all data | Every value contributes |
| Algebraic centre | Deviations sum to zero |
| Sensitive to outliers | Extreme values pull the mean |
| Interval/ratio scale | Requires meaningful numerical distances |

## When to Use the Mean

The mean is most appropriate when:

- Data are approximately normally distributed
- No extreme outliers present
- Interval or ratio scale measurement
- Symmetric distribution

## When to Avoid the Mean

Consider alternatives when:

- Data are heavily skewed (use median)
- Extreme outliers present (use trimmed mean or median)
- Ordinal data (use median)
- Categorical/nominal data (use mode)

## R Code Example

```r
# Calculate mean
mean(scores)

# Mean with missing values
mean(scores, na.rm = TRUE)

# Trimmed mean (removes outliers)
mean(scores, trim = 0.1)  # removes top/bottom 10%
```

## DataLab Connection

The **[Lady Luck](../datalab/lady-luck.qmd)** station tests whether human-generated "random" numbers have the expected mean. If truly random, the mean of 20 numbers (1–10) should be 5.5. Use a one-sample t-test to compare participants' mean to this theoretical value. At the **[Reflex Test](../datalab/reflex-test.qmd)**, calculate mean reaction time across trials, but check for skewness first — RT data often has positive skew.
